content: 1. Food crops intended for processing and fodder crops should be treated with urine or a mixture of urine and water, ensuring a nitrogen concentration of at least 1 g/L. For food crops consumed raw, urine application should occur at least one month before harvesting, and it should be incorporated into the soil if the edible parts grow above the soil surface. 2. Gram-positive bacteria and spore-forming bacteria are not included in the underlying risk assessments, as they are not typically recognized as causes of significant infections. 3. Larger systems involve using urine mixtures to fertilize crops consumed by individuals outside the household from which the urine was collected. Grasslands used for fodder production are excluded from this practice. 4. For all types of treated excreta, additional safety measures are necessary. These include excreta and greywater treatment, crop restrictions, waste application and withholding periods to allow pathogen die-off, hygienic food handling and preparation, health and hygiene promotion, and produce washing, disinfection, and cooking. 5. Workers and their families may be exposed to excreta-related and vector-borne pathogens through activities involving excreta and greywater use. Measures to protect them include personal protective equipment, access to safe drinking water and sanitation facilities, health and hygiene promotion, vector and intermediate host control, and reduced vector contact. 6. Local communities face similar hazards as workers. If they lack access to safe drinking water, they may use contaminated irrigation water for drinking or domestic purposes. Children may also play or swim in contaminated water. Increased vector breeding can lead to vector-borne diseases affecting local communities, even without direct access to the fields. 7. Health protection measures for local communities include excreta and greywater treatment, limited contact during handling, controlled field access, access to safe drinking water and sanitation, health and hygiene promotion, vector and intermediate host control, and reduced vector contact. 8. Monitoring systems serve three purposes: validation (proving the system meets design requirements), operational monitoring (ensuring processes function as expected), and verification (confirming the system achieves specified targets). Validation is performed during system development or when new processes are added. Operational monitoring is routine and relies on simple, quick measurements to address issues promptly. Verification monitoring is periodic and ensures long-term system efficiency. 9. The most effective way to ensure safety in agricultural use of excreta and greywater is through a comprehensive risk assessment and management approach. This includes waste generation, treatment, use as fertilizers or irrigation, and product consumption. Key components include system assessment, identifying control measures, monitoring methods, and developing a management plan. 10. Human behavior significantly influences the transmission of excreta-related diseases. Introducing excreta or greywater use schemes or reducing disease transmission in existing schemes requires assessing the social feasibility of changing behavioral patterns. Cultural beliefs and public perceptions vary widely, and projects can fail if these factors are not adequately addressed. 11. Excreta is a valuable nutrient source for farmers. Its direct use on arable land minimizes environmental impact locally and globally. Reusing excreta secures fertilizers for crop production and reduces negative impacts on water bodies. However, excessive application can lead to nutrient leaching into groundwater or surface water, though this impact is less than direct discharge into water bodies. 12. Phosphorus, essential for plant growth, is often supplied through mined phosphate, but global supplies are diminishing. Approximately 25% of mined phosphorus ends up in aquatic environments or landfills, causing eutrophication. Urine contains over 50% of the phosphorus excreted by humans, and its use in agriculture can enhance crop production while reducing the need for advanced wastewater treatment to remove phosphorus. 13. Economic factors are critical when appraising new projects. Economic analysis establishes feasibility and compares options, including health and environmental impacts on downstream communities. Financial planning determines revenue sources and clarifies payment responsibilities. The profitability of selling products fertilized with excreta or irrigated with greywater also requires analysis. 14. Appropriate policies, legislation, institutional frameworks, and regulations at international, national, and local levels facilitate safe excreta and greywater management. Many countries lack these frameworks. Policies set priorities and allocate resources for implementation through laws, economic measures, education programs, and assignments of rights and responsibilities. 15. National policy frameworks for safe excreta use as fertilizer should define objectives, assess the current policy environment, and develop a national approach. These approaches should integrate into public health programs, including hygiene promotion and access to safe drinking water, and adapt to local sociocultural, environmental, and economic circumstances. 16. Planning and implementing programs for agricultural use of excreta and greywater require a comprehensive, progressive, and incremental approach, addressing the greatest health priorities first. This approach should assess the current sanitary situation and consider local water supply and waste management aspects. Stakeholder involvement and participatory methods are essential for addressing treatment, crop restrictions, waste application, human exposure control, costs, technical aspects, support services, and training.
